body:
Deal: Ubiquiti UniFi Dream Wall All In One Internet Gateway $499 (Was $1889) + Delivery ($0 to Metro Areas/ C&C/ in-Store) @ Scorptec

[Mickey333] Long time stalker, forgot basic rules. Price in the title and I'm not a gentlemen

[cnut] Get your kids to paint on it. Hang it on the fridge.

That's about the weight of a 43" TV. No big deal.
[jeffr] So this beast could be described as a fancy router?
[jeffr] very fancy ! and with backup power too. Even with lots of ports, to use it, you would have to run lots of cables around the house.
[mpember] It has a redundant PSU, but that doesn't mean it will continue to work during a power outage. You still require a separate UPS.
[Shiel B Wright] For a moment there, I thought you mentioned Cardi B's song, among routers and switches.
[Himlord] is this over kill for a standard two-story home? I was looking to get Ubiquiti UniFi U7 Pro Indoor Wireless Access Point for my home ~300$
[DingoBlue] You'd still want 1-3 additional WAPs in addition to the
one built into this thing.
[Himlord] Thx , i have TPlink router AX55 would it be sufficient with Ubiquiti UniFi U7 Pro or do i need more WAPs to cover whole house
[netsurfer] It's an odd combination to go TP-Link router with Ubiquiti UniFi access points. U7 Pro is PoE+ only (you most likely don't have a PoE+ switch so you will need a PoE+ injector). Also, without a controller, most of the advanced features won't be available.
Ubiquiti UniFi setup is generally for people with sufficient ethernet wiring in the house so PoE/PoE+/++ makes sense. WiFi 7 access points with uplink to a WiFi 6 router that only supports 1Gbps LAN ports doesn't make sense either. As for getting it for "future proofing", U7 Pro isn't exactly ideal for WiFi 7 (because it only has a 2.5 Gbps upstream port; you want 10Gbps version). So unless you managed to get a U7 Pro dirt cheap, it is not worth it. I find the U7 "Pro" naming misleading.
The microSD card approach limits the total number of cameras it can support. This one has everything, but not great in any of them (in today's standard).
[kaleidoscope] No matter how powerful, you need multiple points for a good coverage in a multi story house… besides, this contains so many hardwired ports and wifi in same box. I’d personally keep hardwired stuff separated from a wifi point.
Also, comes to mind single point of failure (not that i think this would fail.. my unifi gear are running for 7 years non stop without an incident)
[netsurfer] Having WiFi on an UniFi controller is still a plus, especially if you think about how most people normally do UniFi setup initially (from a mobile phone). I don't have this device, BUT if this one starts without needing to adopt (for the ports; compared to separate switches), that's another advantage. UniFi's product strategy is shrewd and most of us keep buying more UniFi gears.
Single point of failure… UniFi's single controller approach… it doesn't matter which controller you get. That issue is there.
The main issue is gigabit LAN ports and WiFi 6 are no longer the current standards and if you have ethernet wiring nowadays, you want to go for 10Gbps setup (or at least 2.5Gbps setup). Also, you can't use it just as a PoE switch (12 ports PoE, 4 ports without & SFP+ up to 10Gbps).
[eug] Having WiFi on a UniFi controller is still a plus, especially if you think about how some people normally do UniFi setup initially (from a mobile phone).
FWIW initial setup can also be done over Bluetooth the same way. It just appears in the mobile app automatically.
The main issue is gigabit LAN ports and WiFi 6 are no longer the current standards and if you have ethernet wiring nowadays, you want to go for 10Gbps setup (or at least 2.5Gbps setup).
I'd say it really depends on how it'll be used. If it's just for internet access (and CCTV) at home, 1Gbps is plenty for the next few years. Power users who need more than 1Gbps at home right now wouldn't be looking at this sort of all-in-one device anyway. By the time 1Gbps is commonplace it'd probably be time to replace this.
Buying all 10GBps hardware and watching Netflix on an NBN 250 connection would be rather wasteful. And again, power users who want to do high-speed transfers to their NAS all day wouldn't be looking at this sort of all-in-one device anyway.
[netsurfer] @eug: If 1Gbps is good enough, then having WiFi support on this gives you a head start. Even if you need multiple access points, that's still one less to buy.
For people with ethernet wiring throughout the house, honestly 1Gbps setup is not ideal. 2.5Gbps is dirt cheap and more power efficient (even Apple is including 2.5Gbps LAN in the base model of the latest Mac Mini). Proper WiFi 7 routers are essentially all in one. The fact is UniFi likes to milk us multiple times. UDM Pro / SE / Max series really needs an update.
A key advantage of wired setup with access points over mesh is better performance. If the objective is being pragmatic (and aiming for below par NBN 250 (the current sweet spot is NBN 500 price wise)), Ubiquiti UniFi makes no sense. Cheap 10Gbps options are available (if you don't mind second hand Cisco gears). Brand new, there are cheaper options too (just don't get fixated on must run all Ubiquiti gears). One reason you generally need multiple UniFi access points is because most of the cost effective ones have inferior range than low end routers (another way Ubiquiti entices you to buy more or expensive models).
Existing setup, years ago, you had no choice. New setup, buying this to save $$$ on a "new" UniFi setup, that makes no sense. Technically, there is an SFP+ port capable of 10Gbps on this.
[eug] @netsurfer:
If 1Gbps is good enough, then having WiFi support on this gives you a head start. Even if you need multiple access points, that's still one less to buy.
Oh yes definitely. I was just clarifying that wifi isn't needed to setup with a mobile phone.
For people with ethernet wiring throughout the house, honestly 1Gbps setup is not ideal. 2.5Gbps is dirt cheap and more power efficient.
I say it really depends on what they're doing. If the ethernet cabling is for TVs and desktops and APs for internet access, 2.5GBps really isn't adding much to the picture, unless they're planning on upgrading past 1000Mbps internet in the next few years.
Even then, it does have a 10G SFP+ WAN port, a 2.5G WAN port, and a 10G SFP+ port to plug in to a higher-speed switch if it's actually required down the road.
Homes aren't the target market for this device anyway - how many home users need redundant PSUs? I'm pretty sure UI was aiming this at small businesses or stores where all they need is internet access for receiving orders or emails and web browsing, PoE for their VoIP phones and cameras, ethernet for the printer/photocopier/POS, and wifi for a few laptops.
Some homes and home offices also have similar requirements which is probably why people are interested in this for home use too.
If the objective is being pragmatic (and aiming for below par NBN 250 (the current sweet spot is NBN 500 price wise)), Ubiquiti UniFi makes no sense. Cheap 10Gbps options are available (if you don't mind second hand Cisco gears).
Having run Cisco at home in the past and at work, I certainly wouldn't recommend it for a normal home user. The UI experience is the complete polar opposite to UniFi which is the main reason why UniFi is so popular - it's very intuitive to use and easy to set up.
Firmware updates with Cisco is also a pain - depending on the model you can either download it from them or you have to email them and provide them a load of details to request an update, or you need a service contract.
I also ran Meraki for a few years; it's also intuitive but the licensing cost is really prohibitive.
The Dream Wall is definitely not for everyone. There are people who want to run a NAS or have a 2Gbps internet connection at home today, and there also are people who just want to browse the web or receive emails and store documents on O365 in their small office, or just watch Netflix and want good 250-500Mbps wifi coverage at home. Something like this would be perfectly suitable for that for quite a few years. A faster switch can always be added later anyway when the price inevitably drops in a few years time.
[banana365] Gigabit and WiFi 6 absolutely are current standards. Sure, there are newer standards with faster speeds on offer, but I guarantee that anyone asking the basic questions being asked here would not benefit from them.
[Mickey333] Word is this runs on old wifi 6. There is Wifi 7 out but not ubiquiti brand. Maybe do some research b4 buying this
[eug] Also consider what you're using it for. If it's just for internet access and you only have a 250Mbps NBN plan, you might not benefit from the extra speed. There are other benefits too but it might not matter depending on your use.
[whyisave] Wouldn't you also need a controller to use this "Dream Wall" device as well ?
(ie. an added cost)
EDIT:
I found the answer …
Includes full UniFi application suite for device management
[netsurfer] No, if an Ubiquiti UniFi product has the name "Dream" in it, that means it is a controller so you don't need another controller.
[whyisave] There is Wifi 7 out but not ubiquiti brand
You can get WiFi 7 [802.11be] in a "similar form-factor" (box on a wall),
but you will need a controller to manage/connect it all up :
Ubiquiti U7 Pro Wall
- https://techspecs.ui.com/unifi/wifi/u7-pro-wall?subcategory=…
[netsurfer] That's a different category of product.
This one is a controller with integrated PoE(+) switch with 12 ports PoE and 4 port non PoE. The PoE budget on this is quite high and you get a power supply included. It's an old product. The biggest issue is that there were too many cheap gigabit PoE switch deals posted on OZB before and UCG-Fiber is more powerful.
[banana365] Yes, but that's not what the person you're replying to was pointing out. They were correcting the (perhaps poorly phrased) claim that there was no WiFi 7 device from Ubiquiti.

[Mikael] Same. Just wish ports were2.5gb. everything else here either SFP+ or 2.5gb

[whyisave] 128gb SSD and 512gb micro SD
Imagine buying devices, just to shuck their MicroSD and SSDs 😂
[jaada-thendi] I don’t want to imagine; I already did !
[eug] Add a 2.5G Flex Mini for your NAS/PC and use this for internet routing.
[netsurfer] This one has a 10Gbps SFP+ port so UniFi wants you to go for at least the 8 port version of the 2.5G Flex.
Anyone who is serious about NAS would connect the SFP+ port to a 10Gbps switch. The WAN port on this device is 2.5Gbps.
[eug] All the 2.5G devices can plug in to the 2.5G Flex Mini, then that can be uplinked to the Dream Wall's gigabit port for internet access. That way PCs can have high speed connectivity to the NAS and still get 1Gbps internet access.
Of course using the SFP+ port would be the way to go if the internet connection was over 1Gbps. Power users would already know if this is the device for them or not anyway.
Anyone who is serious about NAS would connect the SFP+ port to a 10Gbps switch.
I think anyone who actually needs a 10G network would already know if this product was suitable for them or not. (it probably isn't)
The WAN port on this device is 2.5Gbps.
There are two WAN ports, 10G SFP+ and 2.5GbE.
There is also a separate 10G SFP+ port on the LAN side.
[eug] Do consider how you'll be using the product too. If you don't need high-speed transfers to a NAS, with our regular internet speeds here, 2.5G won't be of any benefit.
Those who actually need 2.5G probably wouldn't be in the market for this sort of all-in-one device anyway - the UCG-Max/UCG Fiber/UDMP Max or similar would probably make more sense for them.
[DingoBlue] Once you have a device like this and can actually see utilisation you will be surprised at how little bandwidth you actually use.
[netsurfer] It does have a SFP+ port capable of 10Gbps. It's WAN port is 2.5Gbps max.
So the problem is basically the same as most if not all UniFi controllers, it has features which make you want to buy more UniFi products (i.e. UniFi switches, which give UniFi a higher profit margin).
[thriftshop] That’s incorrect. The WAN side also has a 10Gbps SFP+ port.
Not that it’s really needed though, as 2.5Gbps is plenty for a WAN port.
[AutomationGuy] I've been waiting for the next deal on the UCG-Fiber. This was tempting…. but want at least 2 RJ45 2.5G ports for NAS. And this is an older processor than the UCG-Fiber too. Can see it being a good deal for somebody - but pretty niche.
[netsurfer] UCG-Fiber is also good from far, but far from good. To get the max out of it, you need a 10Gbps switch (and you most likely will use the SFP+ port). UCG-Fiber's processor is good in theory, but UCG-Fiber cold boot speed is slow and 3GB RAM (same as UCG-Max) crippled its performance (so if you enable Protect and Access as well, you will observe high RAM usage).
[ngengerous] Unreal deal. Finally jumping into the Ubiquiti ecosystem. Thanks OP!
[ngengerous] Appreciate the heads up, but I won't need more than WiFi 6 speeds for the forseeable future - this should do me nicely.
